questions.question: Which of the following is a correct definition of the word 'tributary'?

options.text: A river branching away from another
A river flowing into a larger river
A lake at the rivers mouth
A body of salty water mixing with river water

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**A river flowing into a larger river**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• A **tributary** is defined as a **freshwater** stream or river that feeds into a larger stream, **main-stem river**, or lake.
 
• A **tributary** does not flow directly into the **ocean** or **sea**; instead, its water is collected and carried by the **parent river** toward a larger body of water.
 
• **Statement A**: A river branching away from another is known as a **distributary**, which is the opposite of a tributary and typically occurs in **river deltas**. *Hence, statement A is incorrect.*
 
• **Statement B**: A river flowing into a larger river accurately describes the function of a **tributary**, which contributes its **discharge** to the main river. *Hence, statement B is correct.*
 
• **Statement C**: A lake at a river's mouth is usually referred to as a **lagoon** or a **deltaic lake**, which is a geographical feature formed by **sediment deposition**. *Hence, statement C is incorrect.*
 
• **Statement D**: A body of **salty water** mixing with river water is called an **estuary**, which is a partially enclosed coastal body of **brackish water**. *Hence, statement D is incorrect.*

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Confluence**: This is the specific **geographic point** where two or more bodies of water meet, such as the junction of a **tributary** and the **main river**. A famous example in **India** is the **Devprayag**, where the **Alaknanda** and **Bhagirathi** rivers join to form the **Ganges**.
 
• **Right Bank and Left Bank Tributaries**: Tributaries are categorized based on the side they join the main river when looking **downstream**. For example, the **Yamuna** is a major **right-bank tributary** of the **Ganges**, while the **Gomti** is a **left-bank tributary**.
 
• **River Basin**: Also known as a **drainage basin** or **catchment area**, this includes the total land area drained by a **main river** and all its **tributaries**. The **Amazon Basin** in **South America** is the largest in the world, covering approximately **7 million square kilometers**.
 
• **World Examples**: The **Madeira River** is the largest tributary in the world by volume, flowing into the **Amazon River**. In the **United States**, the **Missouri River** is a massive tributary of the **Mississippi River**.
 
• **Functions**: Tributaries play a critical role in **hydrology** by increasing the **water volume**, **nutrient transport**, and **sediment load** of the parent river, which supports diverse **ecosystems** and **agricultural activities** downstream.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Strahler Stream Order**: This is a **numerical method** used in **hydrology** to rank the size of streams. A **first-order stream** has no tributaries; when two first-order streams join, they form a **second-order stream**, and so on.
 
• **Distributary Characteristics**: Unlike tributaries, **distributaries** are common in the **lower reaches** of a river, particularly in a **delta** like the **Sundarbans** (formed by the **Ganges** and **Brahmaputra**), where the river divides into multiple channels before reaching the **Bay of Bengal**.
 
• **Watershed Divide**: This is the **topographical ridge** or high ground that separates two different **drainage basins**. Precipitation falling on either side of the **divide** will flow into different **tributary systems**.
 
• **Environmental Impact**: Pollution entering a small **tributary** can eventually contaminate the entire **main river** system, making the management of small streams vital for **environmental conservation** and **water security**.

questions.question: In which Indian state is the percussion instrument Davandi primarily found?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Tamil Nadu**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **Davandi** is a traditional **percussion instrument** that is primarily found and used in the **South Indian** state of **Tamil Nadu**.
 
• It is an **hourglass-shaped** drum, belonging to the family of **membranophones**, and is very similar in **features** and **functions** to the **Udukkai**.
 
• This **instrument** is deeply rooted in the **folk music** traditions of **Tamil Nadu** and is a **characteristic** sound in **rural** areas during **religious** ceremonies.
 
• The **Davandi** is often played by **folk performers** and **priests**, particularly during the **worship** of village deities like **Mariamman** or during **Udukkai Pattu** (narrative singing).
 
• The **unique feature** of this **drum** is its **variable pitch**; the **performer** modulates the **sound** by squeezing the **strings** or the cloth **band** around the **middle** of the **instrument** while striking one side.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Construction and Materials:** The **body** of the **Davandi** is traditionally carved from a single piece of **jackfruit wood** or cast in **brass**. The **heads** are covered with **processed goat skin** or **parchment**, which are held in place by **cotton** or **synthetic strings**.
 
• **Geographical Variants:** While **Tamil Nadu** is the primary **location** for the **Davandi**, similar **instruments** exist across **India**. For **example**, the **Damru** is popular in **North India**, and the **Idakka** is a highly sophisticated **hourglass drum** used in **temple** music in **Kerala**.
 
• **Applications in Rituals:** In **Tamil** culture, the **Davandi** or **Udukkai** is frequently used by **Kodangis** (fortune tellers) who **chant** and **drum** to invoke **divine** guidance. It is believed that the **rhythmic** vibrations help in **spiritual** communication.
 
• **Musical Heritage:** **Tamil Nadu** boasts a rich **musical** landscape where **folk instruments** like the **Thavil**, **Parai**, and **Pambai** coexist with **classical** instruments used in **Carnatic music**, such as the **Mridangam**.
 
• **Artistic Features:** The **size** of the **Davandi** can range from **6 inches** to **10 inches** in **length**. Its **portable** nature makes it an **ideal** companion for **itinerant** singers and **street** performers.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Method of Playing:** Unlike the **Mridangam** which is played with both hands, the **Davandi** is typically held in the **left hand** (to control the **pitch** via **compression**) and struck with the **fingers** of the **right hand**.
 
• **Cultural Symbolism:** The **hourglass drum** is often associated with **Lord Shiva** in **Indian** mythology (as the **Damru**), representing the **creation** and **destruction** of the **universe** through **sound**.
 
• **Preservation:** Efforts are being made by the **Government** of **Tamil Nadu** and various **cultural** organizations to preserve **folk** arts like **Udukkai Pattu**, ensuring that the **skill** of making and playing the **Davandi** is passed down to **younger generations**.
 
• **Modern Context:** In **recent years**, many **music directors** in the **Tamil film industry** (Kollywood) have used the **Davandi** in **soundtracks** to provide an **authentic** **rural** and **ethnic** feel to the **music**.

questions.question: The liberalization of the Indian economy in 1991 led to which of the following fiscal outcomes?

options.text: Sharp increase in Government control over pricing
Lowering of direct and indirect tax rates

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Lowering of direct and indirect tax rates**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **liberalization** of the **Indian economy** in **1991** introduced significant fiscal reforms, primarily focusing on the **reduction of tax rates** to encourage compliance and broaden the **tax base**. Hence, the statement regarding the lowering of direct and indirect tax rates is correct.
 
• Tax reforms initiated after **1991** were based on the recommendations of the **Tax Reforms Committee**, also known as the **Raja Chelliah Committee**, which suggested reducing the high rates of **Personal Income Tax** and **Corporate Tax**.
 
• In terms of **Indirect Taxes**, there was a drastic reduction in **Customs Duties** (import duties) to make the Indian economy more integrated with the **global market**. Peak customs duty rates were reduced from over **200%** in **1991** to much lower levels in subsequent years.
 
• The reforms aimed at **simplifying the tax structure** and removing the complexities of the **Excise Duty** system, eventually leading to the implementation of **MODVAT** (Modified Value Added Tax) and later **CENVAT**.
 
• While liberalization aimed at fiscal discipline, it did not lead to the **elimination of all public debt**; in fact, managing **fiscal deficit** remained a challenge for the **Government of India**. Hence, the statement about the elimination of public debt is incorrect.
 
• The **New Economic Policy (NEP)** actually decreased **Government control over pricing** in most sectors (except essential commodities) to allow market forces to determine prices. Hence, the statement about increased control is incorrect.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **New Economic Policy (NEP) of 1991:** Launched during the tenure of Prime Minister **P.V. Narasimha Rao** and Finance Minister **Dr. Manmohan Singh**, the policy was a response to a severe **Balance of Payments (BoP) crisis**.
 
• **LPG Framework:** The reforms are famously known as **Liberalization, Privatization, and Globalization**. **Liberalization** referred to the end of **License Raj**, **Privatization** involved **disinvestment** in **Public Sector Undertakings (PSUs)**, and **Globalization** aimed at opening the **Indian economy** to **Foreign Direct Investment (FDI)**.
 
• **Foreign Exchange Management Act (FEMA):** To facilitate external trade and payments, the stringent **Foreign Exchange Regulation Act (FERA)** of **1973** was eventually replaced by the more liberal **FEMA** in **1999**.
 
• **Industrial Licensing:** Under the **1991 reforms**, **industrial licensing** was abolished for almost all industries, except for a small list of **18 industries** related to security, strategic concerns, and social reasons.
 
• **International Support:** To tide over the **1991 crisis**, India had to borrow from the **International Monetary Fund (IMF)** and the **World Bank**, which came with conditions for **structural adjustments** and **economic stabilization**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Direct Tax Reforms:** Before **1991**, the highest marginal rate of **Income Tax** was very high, which led to **tax evasion**. Post-reforms, the rates were gradually moderated to **10%, 20%, and 30%** slabs to increase **revenue collection**.
 
• **Devaluation of Rupee:** As part of the **fiscal and external sector reforms**, the **Indian Rupee** was devalued twice in **July 1991** to boost **exports** and stabilize the **Balance of Payments**.
 
• **Banking Sector Reforms:** Based on the **Narasimham Committee (1991)** recommendations, the government reduced the **Statutory Liquidity Ratio (SLR)** and **Cash Reserve Ratio (CRR)** to provide more liquidity to the **banking system**.
 
• **MRTP Act:** The **Monopolies and Restrictive Trade Practices (MRTP) Act** was amended to remove the requirement for large companies to seek prior government approval for **expansion** or **establishment of new undertakings**.

questions.question: The administration of the Mauryan Empire is described in which ancient text?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Arthashastra**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **Arthashastra** is an ancient Indian treatise on statecraft, economic policy, and military strategy, written in **Sanskrit**. It is the primary source for understanding the **Mauryan administration**.
 
• The text is traditionally attributed to **Kautilya** (also known as **Chanakya** or **Vishnugupta**), who was the chief advisor and Prime Minister to **Chandragupta Maurya**, the founder of the **Mauryan Empire** in the **4th century BCE**.
 
• It contains **15 books** (Adhikaranas) and **180 sections**, covering a wide range of topics including the duties of the king, **law and justice**, **taxation systems**, **espionage**, and **foreign policy**.
 
• Kautilya introduced the **Saptanga Theory** (Seven Limbs of the State) in this text, which defines the seven essential elements of a kingdom: **Swami** (The King), **Amatya** (The Ministers), **Janapada** (Territory and Population), **Durga** (Fort), **Kosa** (Treasury), **Danda** (Army), and **Mitra** (Ally).
 
• The **Arthashastra** provides evidence of a highly **centralized bureaucracy** and a sophisticated network of **intelligence (spies)**, which were hallmarks of the **Mauryan Empire**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Rigveda**:

 
 
• It is the **oldest** of the four Vedas, composed between **1500 BCE and 1000 BCE** during the **Early Vedic Period**.
 
• The text consists of **1,028 hymns** (Suktas) organized into **10 Mandalas** (books). It focuses on **religious rituals** and the praise of deities like **Agni**, **Indra**, and **Varuna** rather than imperial administration.
 
 
 
• **Mahabharata**:
 
 
• It is one of the two major **Sanskrit epics** of ancient India, traditionally attributed to the sage **Vyasa**.
 
• While it includes the **Shanti Parva**, which contains extensive discussions on **Rajadharma** (the duties of a king), its primary narrative focuses on the struggle between the **Pandavas** and the **Kauravas** at **Kurukshetra**.
 
 
 
• **Manusmriti**:
 
 
• Also known as the **Manava-Dharmashastra**, it is an important legal text and constitution of the **Hindu social system**.
 
• Likely compiled between the **2nd century BCE and 3rd century CE**, it outlines the **Varna system**, social conduct, and **civil and criminal laws**, but it is not specifically a description of the **Mauryan government**.
 
 
 
• **Indica**:
 
 
• Another vital source for **Mauryan history** is **Indica**, written by **Megasthenes**, the Greek ambassador to the court of **Chandragupta Maurya**.
 
• It provides a foreigner's perspective on the **municipal administration** of **Pataliputra** and the **seven-caste system** observed by the Greeks in India.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Administrative Hierarchy**: The Mauryan state was divided into **provinces** headed by a **Kumar** (Prince) or **Aryaputra**. The **Arthashastra** mentions various departments headed by **Adhyakshas** (Superintendents), such as **Panyadhyaksha** (Superintendent of Commerce) and **Sitadhyaksha** (Superintendent of Agriculture).
 
• **Economic Control**: The text emphasizes that **Kosa** (Treasury) is the foundation of the state. It describes elaborate methods for **collecting revenue** from land, forests, mines, and trade to maintain a massive **standing army**.
 
• **Judicial System**: Kautilya describes two types of courts: **Dharmasthiya** (Civil Courts) and **Kantakashodhana** (Criminal Courts), ensuring **law and order** through strict punishments.
 
• **Date and Discovery**: Although the events of the Mauryan Empire occurred in the **4th century BCE**, the manuscript of the **Arthashastra** was rediscovered in **1905** by **R. Shamasastry** in a library in **Mysore**.

questions.question: In a race of 1200 metres, Amit gives Bhushan a head-start of 200 metres. Amit starts 20 seconds after Bhushan. Amit overtakes Bhushan 4 minutes after he (Amit) starts running. Amit finishes the race 10 seconds before Bhushan. What is the running speed (in m/s) of Amit?
questions.solution:
[IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/ca81259519cadfb2d5350673c220e419e60378e9770ad26512fc8e826a8d93f1.png] __Shortcut Trick__

Let speeds = a (Amit), b (Bhushan)

__Overtaking condition:__

Amit runs 240 s ⇒ distance = 240a

Bhushan runs 240 + 20 = 260 s with 200 m head start

⇒ 240a = 200 + 260b ...(1)

__Finishing condition:__

Amit finishes 10 s earlier but started 20 s late ⇒ total gap = 30 s

⇒ 1200/b = 1200/a + 30 ...(2)

From (2):

⇒ 1200(1/b − 1/a) = 30

⇒ (a − b)/ab = 1/40 ...(3)

Solve (1) & (3):

⇒ b = 4

⇒ a = 40/9

**∴ Answer = 40/9 = 4(4)/(9) m/s**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/c76c13ba2d2ab46b47f8a931ae621dac081a0cb266b142dc23f58659fac4a466.png] **__Alternate Method__**

**Given:**

Total distance = 1200 m

Head start = 200 m

Amit starts 20 s late

Overtakes in 240 s

Finishes 10 s earlier

**Formula used:**

Distance = Speed × Time

**Calculation:**

⇒ Overtaking:

240a = 200 + 260b ...(1)

⇒ Finishing:

1200/a + 20 + 10 = 1200/b

⇒ 1200/b = 1200/a + 30 ...(2)

⇒ From (2):

1200(1/b − 1/a) = 30

⇒ (a − b)/ab = 1/40 ...(3)

⇒ Solve (1) and (3):

⇒ b = 4

⇒ a = 40/9

**∴ The correct answer is 40/9 = 4(4)/(9) m/s.**

questions.question: In accordance with Article 84 of the Constitution of India, which of the following is the minimum age a person must meet to qualify for membership of the House of the People?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Twenty-five years**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Article 84** of the **Constitution of India** lays down the qualifications for **membership of Parliament**. It specifies that a person shall not be qualified to be chosen to fill a seat in Parliament unless they meet certain criteria.
 
• According to **Article 84 (b)**, the **minimum age** for a person to become a member of the **House of the People (Lok Sabha)** is **25 years**. ***Hence, Option D is the correct statement.***
 
• The same article specifies that for the **Council of States (Rajya Sabha)**, the **minimum age** required is **30 years**. This ensures a higher age threshold for the Upper House of Parliament.
 
• In addition to age, the person must be a **citizen of India** and must make and subscribe before some person authorized by the **Election Commission** an oath or affirmation according to the form set out for the purpose in the **Third Schedule**.
 
• The candidate must also possess such other qualifications as may be prescribed in that behalf by or under any law made by **Parliament**, such as the **Representation of the People Act, 1951**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **House of the People (Lok Sabha):**

 
 
• It is known as the **Lower House** of India's bicameral Parliament.
 
• Members are **directly elected** by the people on the basis of **Universal Adult Franchise**.
 
• The **maximum strength** of the House envisaged by the Constitution is **552**, though currently, elections are held for **543 seats**.
 
• The normal **tenure** of the Lok Sabha is **5 years** from the date appointed for its first meeting, unless dissolved earlier by the **President**.
 
 
 
• **Council of States (Rajya Sabha):**
 
 
• It is the **Upper House** and represents the States and Union Territories of India.
 
• It is a **permanent body** and is not subject to dissolution; however, **one-third** of its members retire every **second year**.
 
• The **maximum strength** is fixed at **250**, of which **12 members** are nominated by the **President** for their expertise in fields like literature, science, art, and social service.
 
 
 
• **Voting Age (Article 326):**
 
 
• The **minimum age** for **voting** in India is **18 years**. This was reduced from **21 years** by the **61st Constitutional Amendment Act, 1988**, which came into force in **1989**.
 
 
 
• **Local Government Elections:**
 
 
• For elections to **Panchayats** and **Municipalities** (under the **73rd and 74th Amendment Acts**), the **minimum age** for contesting is **21 years**.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Disqualifications (Article 102):** A person shall be disqualified for being chosen as, and for being, a member of either House of Parliament if they hold any **office of profit**, are of **unsound mind**, are an **undischarged insolvent**, or are not a **citizen of India**.
 
• **Representation of the People Act, 1951:** This act adds further requirements, such as the candidate must be registered as an **elector** in any parliamentary constituency.
 
• **The President:** While the **President** is a part of Parliament (along with the two houses), the minimum age to be eligible for election as President of India is **35 years** as per **Article 58**.
 
• **The Vice-President:** Similarly, **Article 66** stipulates that the **minimum age** to serve as **Vice-President** (who is the ex-officio Chairman of the Rajya Sabha) is also **35 years**.

questions.question: The interference of two identical waves moving in opposite directions produces:
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Standing Waves**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• When two identical waves (having the same **frequency**, **wavelength**, and **amplitude**) travel through the same medium in **opposite directions** and interfere with each other, they produce **Standing Waves** (also known as **Stationary Waves**). ***Hence, the correct option is Standing Waves.***
 
• Unlike traveling waves, **Standing Waves** do not transport **energy** from one end of the medium to the other; instead, the energy remains localized within the vibration pattern.
 
• The specific points in the wave pattern that remain **stationary** and have **zero amplitude** are called **Nodes**. These occur due to **destructive interference**.
 
• The points that undergo maximum displacement and have the **largest amplitude** are called **Antinodes**. These occur due to **constructive interference**.
 
• The distance between two consecutive **Nodes** or two consecutive **Antinodes** is exactly **λ/2** (half the wavelength), while the distance between a **Node** and its adjacent **Antinode** is **λ/4**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Longitudinal Waves**: In these waves, the particles of the medium vibrate **parallel** to the direction of the wave's propagation. Common examples include **sound waves** in air and **seismic P-waves**. These waves consist of **compressions** and **rarefactions**. ***Hence, statement A is incorrect.***
 
• **Transversal Waves**: In these waves, the particles of the medium move **perpendicularly** to the direction of wave travel. Examples include **light waves**, **radio waves**, and waves on a **plucked guitar string**. These waves consist of **crests** and **troughs**. ***Hence, statement C is incorrect.***
 
• **Incident Waves**: An **incident wave** is the initial wave that strikes a boundary or an interface between two different media. It is not a result of interference but rather a component that participates in it. ***Hence, statement B is incorrect.***
 
• **Superposition Principle**: This principle states that when two or more waves overlap, the resulting **displacement** is the algebraic sum of the individual displacements of the waves. This is the fundamental mechanism behind the formation of **standing waves**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Applications**: **Standing waves** are essential in the functioning of musical instruments. For example, in **stringed instruments** like the violin or piano, standing waves are formed on a **stretched string** fixed at both ends. In **wind instruments** like the flute or organ pipes, they are formed within **air columns**.
 
• **Harmonics and Overtones**: The simplest standing wave pattern is the **fundamental frequency** (first harmonic). Higher-frequency patterns are called **overtones** or **higher harmonics**, which are **integer multiples** of the fundamental frequency.
 
• **Mathematical Condition**: For a string of length **L** fixed at both ends, the possible wavelengths for standing waves are given by the formula **λ = 2L/n**, where **n** is a positive **integer** (1, 2, 3...).
 
• **Medium Constraints**: The formation of **standing waves** often requires the wave to be **confined** within a specific region (like a pipe or a string), leading to the **reflection** of waves which then interfere with the **incoming waves**.

questions.question: Which of the following best explains the difference between weather and climate?

options.text: Weather refers to short-term changes; climate refers to long-term patterns
Weather refers to long-term trends; climate refers to short-term changes
Weather and climate mean exactly the same phenomenon
Weather is permanent in nature; climate is temporary in nature

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Weather refers to short-term changes; climate refers to long-term patterns**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Weather** is the state of the **atmosphere** at a particular **place** and **time** as regards heat, cloudiness, dryness, sunshine, wind, and rain. It refers to the **short-term** atmospheric conditions that can change within **minutes**, **hours**, or **days**.
 
• **Climate** is defined as the **average** of the weather patterns in a **region** over a **long period of time**. According to the **World Meteorological Organization (WMO)**, the standard period used to determine the climate of a **location** is **30 years**.
 
• The primary components that define both weather and climate include **temperature**, **humidity**, **precipitation**, **atmospheric pressure**, **wind speed**, and **solar radiation**.
 
• While **weather** is what you see outside on any particular **day**, **climate** is the description of the **long-term** pattern of weather in a particular **area**. For **example**, a **thunderstorm** is a weather event, but a **tropical rainforest** has a **hot and humid climate**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Meteorology:** This is the **scientific study** of the **atmosphere** that focuses on **weather processes** and **forecasting**. Scientists in this field, known as **meteorologists**, use **numerical models** and **satellite data** to predict **short-term** changes.
 
• **Climatology:** This branch of **science** deals with the **description** of **climates** and the **analysis** of the causes of **climatic changes**. It examines **long-term** trends such as **global warming** and **ice ages**.
 
• **Climate Zones:** The **Earth** is divided into different **climatic zones** based on **latitude**, such as the **Tropical zone**, **Temperate zone**, and **Polar zone**. Factors like **altitude**, **distance from the sea**, and **ocean currents** also significantly influence the **local climate**.
 
• **Climate Change:** This refers to **long-term shifts** in **temperatures** and **weather patterns**. While these shifts may be **natural**, since the **1800s**, **human activities** (primarily the burning of **fossil fuels**) have been the main driver of **climate change**.
 
• **Instruments:** Common **tools** used to measure weather include the **thermometer** (temperature), **barometer** (pressure), **anemometer** (wind speed), and **hygrometer** (humidity).

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Statement A:** This correctly identifies that **weather** is **short-term** (variable) and **climate** is **long-term** (stable average). **Hence, statement A is correct.**
 
• **Statement B:** This statement incorrectly swaps the definitions, suggesting weather is **long-term**. **Hence, statement B is incorrect.**
 
• **Statement C:** While **weather** and **climate** are related, they represent different **time scales** and **statistical measures**. **Hence, statement C is incorrect.**
 
• **Statement D:** **Weather** is **temporary** and **dynamic**, while **climate** is relatively **constant** over decades but can change over **centuries**; neither is strictly "permanent." **Hence, statement D is incorrect.**

questions.question: Which of the following separates the Andaman from Nicobar Islands?
questions.solution:

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **Ten Degree Channel** is a body of water that separates the **Andaman Islands** and **Nicobar Islands** from each other in the **Bay of Bengal**. ***Hence, the option Ten Degree Channel is correct.***
 
• It is named so because it lies on the **10-degree line of latitude** north of the **equator**.
 
• Specifically, this channel separates **Little Andaman** in the north from **Car Nicobar** in the south.
 
• The channel has a width of approximately **150 kilometers** (about **93 miles**) from north to south and is oriented in an east-west direction.
 
• It serves as a major **maritime route** for ships moving through the **Andaman Sea**, providing a safe passage for international trade and **shipping** vessels.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Palk Strait:**

 
 
• The **Palk Strait** is a strait between the **Tamil Nadu** state of **India** and the **Mannar** district of the Northern Province of **Sri Lanka**.
 
• It connects the **Bay of Bengal** in the northeast with **Palk Bay** in the southwest.
 
• The strait is named after **Robert Palk**, who was a governor of **Madras Presidency** during the **Company Raj** period. ***Hence, this option is incorrect.***
 
 
 
• **Nine Degree Channel:**
 
 
• The **Nine Degree Channel** is located in the **Indian Ocean** and separates the island of **Minicoy** from the main **Lakshadweep** archipelago.

• **Six Degree Channel:**
 
 
• Also known as the **Great Channel**, it is located between the **Great Nicobar Island** of India and the **Sumatra** island of **Indonesia**.
 
• It is a significant **international shipping lane** used by tankers and cargo ships moving towards the **Strait of Malacca**. ***Hence, this option is incorrect.***
 
 
 
• **Eight Degree Channel:**
 
 
• This channel separates the islands of **Minicoy** (the southernmost island of **Lakshadweep**, India) and the **Maldives**.
 
• It is located at the **8° N latitude** and serves as a maritime boundary between the two nations.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Andaman and Nicobar Geography:** The **Andaman and Nicobar Islands** is a **Union Territory** of India comprising **572 islands**, out of which only about **38** are permanently inhabited.
 
• **Volcanic Activity:** **Barren Island**, located in the **Andaman Sea**, is the only confirmed **active volcano** in **South Asia**. Its first recorded eruption dates back to **1787**.
 
• **Highest Peak:** **Saddle Peak** is the highest point in the archipelago, standing at **732 meters**, located in **North Andaman**.

questions.question: If a = x + (2)/(x) and b = x - (2)/(x), then find the value of a⁴ + b⁴ - 2a²b².
questions.solution:
[IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/ca81259519cadfb2d5350673c220e419e60378e9770ad26512fc8e826a8d93f1.png] __Shortcut Trick__

a = x + 2/x, b = x − 2/x

a² − b² = (a − b)(a + b)

⇒ a − b = 4/x, a + b = 2x

⇒ a² − b² = (4/x)(2x) = 8

a⁴ + b⁴ − 2a²b² = (a² − b²)²

⇒ = 8² = 64

**∴ Answer = 64**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/c76c13ba2d2ab46b47f8a931ae621dac081a0cb266b142dc23f58659fac4a466.png] **__Alternate Method__**

**Given:**

a = x + 2/x, b = x − 2/x

**Concept Used:**

a⁴ + b⁴ − 2a²b² = (a² − b²)²

**Calculation:**

⇒ a − b = (x + 2/x) − (x − 2/x) = 4/x

⇒ a + b = (x + 2/x) + (x − 2/x) = 2x

⇒ a² − b² = (a − b)(a + b)

⇒ = (4/x)(2x) = 8

⇒ (a² − b²)² = 8² = 64

**∴ The correct answer is 64.**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **__Additional Information__**

questions.question: Kalamkari painting involves the use of which instrument for drawing outlines?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Bamboo pen**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Kalamkari** is a world-renowned traditional **Indian** art form that involves hand-painting or block-printing on **cotton** textiles. The term is derived from the **Persian** words "**Kalam**" (meaning pen) and "**Kari**" (meaning craftsmanship), literally translating to "pen-work."
 
• The primary instrument used for drawing the intricate outlines in this art form is a **bamboo pen** or a **date palm stick**. This **bamboo stick** is sharpened at one end to create a fine tip for precision, while a piece of **wool** or **cloth** is tied just above the tip to act as a reservoir for the liquid dye.
 
• The **Srikalahasti style** of Kalamkari, practiced in the **Chittoor** district of **Andhra Pradesh**, is entirely dependent on the **bamboo pen**. Artisans use the **Kalam** to freehand sketch complex scenes from **Hindu mythology**, including the **Ramayana**, **Mahabharata**, and **Puranas**, directly onto the fabric.
 
• A distinctive feature of Kalamkari is the exclusive use of **natural dyes** and **vegetable colors**. To obtain the color **black**, artisans mix **jaggery**, **iron filings**, and **water**; for **red**, they use the **madder root**; and for **yellow**, **pomegranate rinds** or **myrobalan** flowers are used.
 
• The process of making a Kalamkari painting is extremely labor-intensive, involving up to **23 steps**. These steps include **bleaching** the cloth using **cow dung**, treating it with **milk** and **myrobalan** (to prevent the dye from spreading), sketching with the **bamboo pen**, and multiple rounds of **washing** in running river water.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Regional Variations:** There are two main styles of Kalamkari in **India**. The **Srikalahasti style** is characterized by freehand drawing with the **Kalam**, whereas the **Machilipatnam style** (from **Krishna** district) primarily uses **wooden blocks** for printing the main designs, though the **bamboo pen** is still used for finer details and filling colors.
 
• **Historical Evolution:** The art form flourished during the **17th century** under the patronage of the **Golconda Sultanate** and the **Mughal Empire**. It was later supported by the **British**, who referred to these printed fabrics as "**Chintz**." In **2007**, **Srikalahasti Kalamkari** was granted the **Geographical Indication (GI) tag**, recognizing its unique cultural origin.
 
• **Material Science:** The fabric used is generally **hand-processed cotton**. The cloth is first treated with a "**mordant**" solution made from **Myrobalan** (Karaka Puvvu) and **buffalo milk**. The **fats** in the milk prevent the dye from bleeding into the fabric fibers, ensuring that the **Kalam** strokes remain sharp and defined.
 
• **Ecological Significance:** Unlike modern synthetic prints, Kalamkari is **eco-friendly**. Every stage of the process utilizes **natural resources**. For instance, **alum** is used as a fixing agent to ensure the **natural dyes** adhere to the **cotton** fibers permanently, making the fabric resistant to fading.
 
• **Applications and Modern Use:** Historically used for temple **hangings** and **scrolls**, Kalamkari is now applied to **saris**, **dupattas**, and **home decor** items. It remains a vital source of livelihood for thousands of artisans in **Andhra Pradesh** and continues to be a symbol of **India's** rich textile heritage in the **global fashion** industry.

questions.question: What was the dominant type of economy in the Harappan heartland?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Agro-pastoral**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The Harappan civilization, also known as the **Indus Valley Civilization**, existed approximately between **2600 BCE and 1900 BCE**. While it was a highly urbanized society, its economic foundation was rooted in an **Agro-pastoral** system.
 
• Agriculture was the primary occupation in the **Harappan heartland** (the fertile plains of the **Indus** and **Ghaggar-Hakra** rivers). The farmers produced a surplus of food grains, which was essential to sustain the non-agricultural urban populations.
 
• **Animal husbandry** or **pastoralism** was equally significant. The Harappans domesticated a variety of animals, including **humped cattle (Zebu)**, **buffalo**, **sheep**, and **goats**, which provided milk, meat, and labor for tilling fields.
 
• Major crops cultivated included **wheat**, **barley**, **lentils**, **chickpeas**, and **sesame**. Evidence of **millets** has been found in sites located in **Gujarat**, while **rice** husks were discovered at **Lothal** and **Rangpur**.
 
• The technology used for farming included the **wooden plough**, as evidenced by terracotta models found at **Banawali** and **ploughed field** marks discovered at **Kalibangan** in **Rajasthan**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Geographical Context:** The Harappan heartland spanned across modern-day **Pakistan** (provinces of **Sindh** and **Punjab**) and **North-Western India** (states of **Gujarat**, **Rajasthan**, and **Haryana**). The proximity to river systems allowed for **alluvial soil** farming.
 
• **Trade-based Economy:** While trade was a vital component of their wealth, it was not the "type" of economy but rather a functional branch. Harappans engaged in **internal and external trade** with **Mesopotamia** (referred to as **Meluha**), **Oman**, and **Afghanistan** for minerals and luxury items like **Lapis Lazuli**.
 
• **Irrigation:** Most Harappan sites were located in semi-arid lands. To manage water, they utilized **canals** (found at **Shortughai** in **Afghanistan**) and **wells**. The **Dholavira** site in **Gujarat** is famous for its sophisticated **water reservoirs**.
 
• **Non-Dominant Economic Types:**
 
 
• **Hunting-gathering:** While Harappans did hunt wild animals like **boar** and **deer**, and consumed **fish**, they were not a nomadic hunting-gathering society; they were settled agriculturists.
 
• **Spiritual-centric:** Although religion played a role in social cohesion (as seen in the **Great Bath** or **Fire Altars**), the economy was driven by material production and resource management rather than spiritual rituals.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Cotton Cultivation:** The Harappans were likely the first people to grow **cotton** (known as **Sindon** to the Greeks). This led to the development of a **textile industry**, which became a major export commodity.
 
• **Granaries:** The discovery of massive **granaries** at **Mohenjo-Daro** and **Harappa** indicates that the state or the elite controlled the collection and distribution of **agricultural surplus**, possibly as a form of **taxation**.
 
• **Standardization:** The economy was supported by a highly standardized system of **weights and measures**. They used **chert** stones for cubical weights, which followed a **binary** and **decimal** system (1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, etc.).
 
• **Seal Usage:** **Steatite seals** featuring animal motifs and a yet-to-be-deciphered **script** were used primarily for **commercial transactions** to mark goods and verify the identity of the sender.
 
• **Storage Technology:** In the **Gujarat** region, **pastoralism** was more dominant than in the northern plains because the land was better suited for **cattle rearing**, which supplied the urban centers with dairy and leather products.
